title: Common Errors, Organized by Pattern
shortDescription: A single reference sheet of WRONG → WHY → CORRECT, grouped by the same error patterns exams reuse year after year.
genZNote: Exams recycle the same handful of traps in different costumes. Learn the pattern once, catch it every time it returns.

sections.heading: Agreement errors
bullets: WRONG: 'Each of the boys have done their work.' → WHY: 'each' is singular. → CORRECT: 'Each of the boys HAS done his work.' MEMORY HOOK: each, every, either, neither = always singular.

WRONG: 'The number of accidents are increasing.' → WHY: 'the number of' takes a singular verb. → CORRECT: 'The number of accidents IS increasing.' MEMORY HOOK: 'A number' = many (plural); 'THE number' = one figure (singular).

sections.heading: Article errors
bullets: WRONG: 'He is an European.' → WHY: 'European' starts with a consonant SOUND ('yuro-'). → CORRECT: 'He is A European.' MEMORY HOOK: sound, not spelling, decides a/an.
WRONG: 'She plays the cricket every evening.' → WHY: games take no article. → CORRECT: 'She plays cricket every evening.' MEMORY HOOK: games = zero article; musical instruments = 'the'.

sections.heading: Preposition errors
bullets: WRONG: 'We must discuss about this problem.' → WHY: 'discuss' already means 'talk about'; adding 'about' is redundant/non-standard. → CORRECT: 'We must discuss this problem.' MEMORY HOOK: discuss NEVER takes 'about'.
WRONG: 'He is married with an actress.' → WHY: 'married' pairs fixedly with 'to'. → CORRECT: 'He is married TO an actress.' MEMORY HOOK: married TO, not married WITH.

sections.heading: Tense errors
bullets: WRONG: 'I am living in this city since 2015.' → WHY: 'since' needs a perfect (not simple/continuous-only) tense. → CORRECT: 'I HAVE BEEN LIVING in this city since 2015.' MEMORY HOOK: since/for + present perfect (continuous).

WRONG: 'If it will rain, we will stay home.' → WHY: if-clauses use present tense for future meaning. → CORRECT: 'If it RAINS, we will stay home.' MEMORY HOOK: no 'will' inside if/when/before/until clauses.

sections.heading: Pronoun errors
bullets: WRONG: 'Everyone must submit their ID proof to him or her respective department.' → WHY: mismatched/mixed pronoun reference. → CORRECT: 'Everyone must submit HIS OR HER ID proof to HIS OR HER respective department' (or accepted modern usage: 'their...their', kept consistent). MEMORY HOOK: keep the same pronoun choice throughout a sentence.

WRONG: 'Ram told Shyam that he had lost his job.' (ambiguous 'he') → WHY: unclear antecedent. → CORRECT: Rephrase to name who lost the job directly: 'Ram told Shyam, "I have lost my job."' MEMORY HOOK: if a pronoun could point to two people, the sentence needs rewriting, not just fixing.

sections.heading: Redundancy and parallelism errors
bullets: WRONG: 'Please return back the book by tomorrow.' → WHY: 'return' already means 'go/give back'. → CORRECT: 'Please return the book by tomorrow.' MEMORY HOOK: return, revert, repeat never need 'back'/'again' attached.

WRONG: 'She likes reading, writing, and to paint.' → WHY: mixed grammatical forms in a list. → CORRECT: 'She likes reading, writing, and painting.' MEMORY HOOK: match the form of every item in a list.

sections.heading: Modifier and word-choice errors
bullets: WRONG: 'She sings good.' → WHY: a verb needs an adverb, not an adjective. → CORRECT: 'She sings WELL.' MEMORY HOOK: good describes a noun; well describes an action.

WRONG: 'This is the most unique idea I have heard.' → WHY: 'unique' is an absolute adjective; it can't be intensified. → CORRECT: 'This is a UNIQUE idea I have heard.' MEMORY HOOK: unique, perfect, complete = no 'more/most' before them.

quickRevision.oneLineDefinition: The recurring exam error families — agreement, articles, prepositions, tense, pronoun reference, redundancy/parallelism, and modifier/word choice — repeat across papers in different sentences but the same underlying rule.
keyFacts: Most 'spot the error' questions are a rephrasing of one of a small number of recurring rule violations.
Learning the WRONG → WHY → CORRECT → MEMORY HOOK chain for each pattern generalises to unfamiliar sentences testing the same rule.

highYieldFacts: 'Discuss about', 'return back', 'married with', and 'each...have' are among the single most repeated wrong forms across competitive English papers.
commonTraps: Treating every sentence as unique instead of matching it to a known error pattern first.
mustRemember: Before assuming 'no error', actively test the sentence against each error-pattern family in turn.
possibleQuestions: Spot the error and correct it: 'He returned back home late at night.'
Spot the error and correct it: 'Neither of the two options are correct.'
